analysis.one_liner: Restricts federal absentee voting to people with a specific excuse, verified by sworn application.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote in the House; it died in committee at the end of the 118th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have changed federal law so that a state could only give you an absentee ballot for a federal election if you had one of a few accepted excuses: your job prevents you from voting in person, you are a full-time caregiver, you have a disability or illness that keeps you from the polls, you will be out of town, or another federal law entitles you to one. You would have to apply in writing with a sworn statement of your identity and your reason, and the application would have to arrive by noon on the Friday before the election. The bill was introduced in May 2024, sent to the House Administration Committee, never received a hearing or a vote, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be candidates and parties that benefit from lower overall turnout, since requiring an excuse and a sworn application with a midday-Friday deadline would shrink the pool of mail voters. Election officials would face no new benefit; the bill imposes verification work on them. The bill primarily restricts access rather than directing resources to any group.

how_it_helps.text: For the voters it serves, the bill would narrow federal absentee voting to a fixed list of excuses and require a sworn statement on each application, which its sponsor presents as a safeguard for election integrity.

analysis.who_pays: Voters who cannot easily get to a polling place: workers whose schedules are not formally protected, caregivers, older voters, and people with disabilities, plus voters who miss the noon-Friday application deadline. Election offices would also bear the cost of reviewing excuses and sworn statements on every application.
analysis.who_pays_short: Voters who can't reach the polls easily

drawbacks.text: Voters would have to state and swear to a specific excuse (work, caregiving, disability, travel) just to get a mail ballot, and applications could not be filed after noon on the Friday before the election.
Voters with inflexible jobs, chronic illness, or caregiving duties could lose the option of voting by mail; many states currently allow no-excuse absentee voting for any voter.
Election officials would have to review and verify an excuse and sworn statement on every absentee application, adding cost and delay without addressing any demonstrated failure in the record.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stated goal—uniform integrity standards for federal absentee ballots—is modest, and the bill would have imposed some real administrative burden on states and voters with little evidence in the record of a matching problem. The costs fall on voters who cannot easily reach a polling place, and the burdens fall hardest on those with the least schedule flexibility. On balance, the drawbacks outweigh the stated benefit.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Administration Committee in May 2024, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced May 22, 2024, the bill was referred to the House Committee on House Administration and received no further action.
No other member signed on as a cosponsor.
The bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, without a committee vote or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Voters who rely on no-excuse or broad absentee voting—older voters, people with disabilities, shift workers, and caregivers—kept the access they have, because the restriction never became law. No interest loses anything material from the bill's failure.

for.name: Rep. Glenn Grothman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to restrict federal absentee voting to voters with a qualifying excuse, verified by sworn application.

sides.party_line_note: Only one member, a Republican, was ever attached to the bill, and no vote was ever taken, so no party split can be measured.
